tldr: We propose GlobMP, a new continuous-time motion planner that strictly satisfies nonlinear constraints such as collision avoidance and learned policy tracking at every instant of the motion, while provably converging to a globally optimal solution by refining piecewise-polynomial curves.
hero_caption: Overview of steering on a bimanual humanoid. A high-level meta-reasoner (VLM) defines geometric constraints once. The planner (GlobMP) then continuously steers the learned policy's proposed trajectory to satisfy all constraints at every instant, smoothly controlling the physical robot.
overview:
In robotics, motion planning—generating smooth trajectories while avoiding collisions with obstacles—is one of the most fundamental and critical challenges. In recent years, it has also been widely used as a steering technique to correct motions proposed by machine learning-based generative models and policies so they satisfy safety constraints. However, conventional methods suffer from critical gaps. Methods that check constraints by sampling time finely can miss collisions that occur between sample points. Methods that convexify free space cannot leverage the full extent of the non-convex environment. Semidefinite relaxations (SDP) cannot guarantee global optimality unless the relaxation happens to be tight.

To solve this, the authors represent trajectories as piecewise-polynomial curves (such as Bézier curves) and reframe the condition that constraint values remain nonnegative over the entire time interval $[0,1]$ as a projection problem onto the closed convex cone of nonnegative polynomials. They propose GlobMP (Global Motion Planning), which alternates between gradient descent on the objective cost and projection onto the feasible set. They theoretically prove that, as the number of polynomial pieces $N$ increases, GlobMP asymptotically converges to the continuous-time global optimum within any chosen constraint tolerance.

In experiments, the authors evaluated GlobMP on dense cross-over tasks with up to 200 multi-robot agents, decentralized navigation on the physical Robotarium testbed, and daily manipulation tasks with a bimanual humanoid equipped with tactile sensors. Even in dense environments where sampling and conventional trajectory optimization baselines fail, GlobMP achieved nearly 100% safe navigation and substantially improved the contact-control performance of learned policies.
contributions: Formulated a continuous-time optimization problem that strictly satisfies collision avoidance, inter-robot separation, and steering constraints at every instant over the entire interval $[0,1]$ in a unified manner using polynomial nonnegative cone constraints.
Proposed GlobMP, an algorithm that alternates between cost gradient steps and convex feasibility restoration steps.
Theoretically proved global convergence: under mild assumptions, GlobMP converges to the continuous-time global optimum as the number of polynomial pieces increases.

Demonstrated superior performance over strong baselines across simulations with up to 200 robots, multi-robot swarm control on the physical Robotarium testbed, and real-world tactile manipulation on a bimanual humanoid.

sections.heading: How do we bridge the sampling gap? The challenge of continuous-time planning
sections.summary: Motion planning is widely used from navigation to correcting learned policy trajectories, but it faces issues such as missing collisions between discrete samples and lacking global optimality guarantees. This work proposes GlobMP, a continuous-time planner that guarantees constraint satisfaction at every instant while provably converging to the global optimum.
sections.details:
When finding a smooth trajectory for a robot from start to goal, one must avoid collisions while minimizing a smoothness cost (such as the integral of squared acceleration or snap). However, traditional sampling-based methods (like RRT*) often cause collisions during path smoothing, and trajectory optimization methods (like TrajOpt) tend to get trapped in local minima. In particular, collocation methods that enforce constraints only at finely discretized time steps cannot prevent "intersample collisions," where the robot clips an obstacle between sample points.

Furthermore, there is growing demand for "steering" to pull trajectories generated by learned diffusion models back into safe regions. Yet, to date, no algorithm has provably converged to a globally optimal motion once a smoothness cost is combined with non-convex collision constraints over the entire continuous-time interval.

The authors cast collision avoidance with moving obstacles and other robots, as well as steering constraints to stay close to reference trajectories, into a single continuous-time optimization problem $(P_\infty)$. By treating trajectories as curves in a Sobolev space $\mathcal{H}^k$ and combining piecewise-polynomial representations with projections onto nonnegative cones, they close the discretization gap and open a pathway to the global optimum.

sections.heading: Solving via polynomial geometry: Alternating cone projection and gradient descent
sections.summary: By expressing trajectories in a Bernstein polynomial basis, constraint satisfaction over all time is converted into a membership problem in a convex cone for the coefficient vectors. GlobMP searches for solutions by alternating between gradient steps that reduce cost and restoration steps that pull violated constraints back into the convex cone.
sections.details:
### Polynomial Representation and Reduction to the Nonnegative Cone
The trajectory $\bm{\gamma}(t)$ is represented as a Bernstein polynomial of degree $d$. Constraints $g_j(\bm{\gamma}(t), t) \geq 0$, such as squared distances to obstacles or closeness to a reference trajectory, become polynomials in time $t \in [0, 1]$. The condition that this polynomial remains nonnegative over the entire time interval is equivalent to its coefficient vector $\bm{\pi}_j$ belonging to the "closed convex cone of nonnegative polynomials $\mathcal{K}$." The key insight is that rather than simply checking if individual coefficients are positive, testing cone membership accurately determines true nonnegativity without missing negative dips.

### How the GlobMP Algorithm Works
Boundary conditions (fixed position, velocity, etc. at start and goal) are expressed as linear equality constraints on the control points. Using a nullspace basis $\mathbf{N}$, the problem is transformed into free variables $\bm{\Gamma}_{\mathrm{free}}$, ensuring boundary conditions are always strictly met. GlobMP alternates between two steps:
- **Cost reduction step**: Updates control points along the gradient direction of the smoothness objective (the integral of squared acceleration or snap).
- **Feasibility restoration step (Algorithm 2)**: For blocks violating constraints, computes the minimal projection residual onto the convex cone $\mathcal{K}_j$ and pushes the control points back toward constraint satisfaction via the Jacobian.

The projection onto the convex cone itself is solved rapidly as a small convex optimization (a Frank-Wolfe-style greedy algorithm) using the dual cone basis, scaling linearly with the number of blocks.

sections.heading: Why does it reach the global optimum? Convergence by increasing piece counts
sections.summary: The authors theoretically prove that starting from an initial grid with a fine step size and increasing the number of polynomial pieces $N$ asymptotically reaches the continuous-time global optimum to any desired precision. On stable instances, it yields the exact global optimum.
sections.details:
### Framework for Global Convergence (Theorem 1)
Although collision constraints are non-convex with respect to the control points, they are convex in the robot positions. Consequently, linearizations at the control points always lie beneath the true constraint. Leveraging this property, the restoration step is analyzed using the local convex feasible set $\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{z})$ constructed at each iteration.

The main theoretical result (Theorem 1) establishes the following:
- Starting from a feasible point, GlobMP iterations preserve continuous-time feasibility and monotonically decrease the objective value.
- In the spline space $\mathcal{S}_N$ of $N$ polynomial pieces, picking the lowest-cost point from a control point grid as the start guarantees that, as $N \to \infty$, the objective value approaches the global optimum $E^\star_\infty$ of the continuous-time problem $(P_\infty)$.
- When allowing a constraint tolerance $\mu > 0$, the suboptimality gap decreases at the rate $\delta_N = C N^{-r}$, with constraint violations bounded below $\mu$.

### Specific Convergence Rates
For instance, in minimum-snap trajectory planning ($k=4$) with boundary conditions fixed up to jerk ($\ell=3$), the number of pieces $N$ required to achieve an accuracy $\varepsilon$ is only $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2/7})$. If snap itself is fixed at the boundaries ($\ell=k$), the boundary correction cost leads to $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-1})$. In either case, the ability to capture the global optimum with polynomial complexity is a major strength.

sections.heading: From 200-robot swarms to bimanual humanoids: Superior real-world safety
sections.summary: GlobMP was evaluated on synthetic cross-over tasks with up to 200 robots, 12-robot physical runs on Robotarium, and daily manipulation tasks with a tactile-equipped bimanual humanoid. In dense settings where existing trajectory optimizers and generative planners collide, GlobMP achieved 100% continuous-time safety.
sections.details:
### Synthetic Experiments: Large-Scale Swarms of up to 200 Robots
The authors evaluated a dense task where robots swap positions in a space populated with spherical obstacles. Compared against baselines such as RRT*, GCS (Graphs of Convex Sets), and SDP-MP (semidefinite relaxation), the baselines' collision rates surged as the robot count grew, failing entirely on all trials with 16 or more robots. In contrast, GlobMP achieved zero collisions across all time $t$ on all instances from 2 up to 200 robots (approximately 82,000 constraint blocks). Even for the massive 200-robot scenario, it computed solutions in just 28 seconds on a GPU (2 minutes on a CPU).

### Real-Robot Swarm Verification (Robotarium)
Experiments were conducted on the Robotarium at Georgia Tech (a 3.2m × 2.0m arena) using differential-drive GRITSBot robots. Up to 12 robots navigated dense cross-over scenarios across 5 benchmark obstacle environments. While recent diffusion-based planners (such as DiRecT and PCD-SHD) suffered frequent collisions with walls and other robots as agent counts increased (e.g., all robots colliding in a 12-robot ring test), GlobMP maintained a minimum clearance of at least 6 cm at all times and achieved a near-perfect task success rate.

### Tactile Steering on a Real Bimanual Humanoid
Using a Dexmate Vega-1 (38 degrees of freedom across arms and hands), the authors evaluated steering trajectories proposed by pretrained VLA policies (GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$). They performed four contact-rich tasks: tissue pulling, object handover, and shelf placement. A large language model (Claude Opus 5.5) defined stay-out and grasping constraints once from scene images, and GlobMP continuously steered the policy's chunked output as a reference trajectory at 30 Hz. While the standalone policy failed on tissue pulling and handovers under out-of-distribution observations, adding GlobMP steered every trial to success.

captions.F6: Trajectories of 12 physical robots crossing paths on the Robotarium. Existing methods (such as DiRecT and Final Proj.) exhibit numerous collisions near the central obstacle (red boxes), whereas GlobMP (far right) routes every robot smoothly to its goal with zero collisions.
captions.F11: Hardware runs of 12 GRITSBots in the Conveyor environment. The minimum clearance between obstacles and robots is maintained at 6 cm across all time, strictly avoiding contact even during dense passings.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook: New horizons in robotics through continuous-time global guarantees
sections.summary: GlobMP is a breakthrough framework that simultaneously provides strict continuous-time constraint satisfaction and global convergence guarantees. Its practical utility and high reliability were demonstrated in multi-agent robot navigation and complex manipulation.
sections.details:
This paper established GlobMP, a motion planner that guarantees continuous-time constraint satisfaction and convergence to global optima by combining piecewise-polynomial curves with projections onto nonnegative cones. It provides both theoretical and practical answers to long-standing challenges, such as inter-sample collisions and getting trapped in local minima.

In particular, it serves as an external steering module that reliably addresses the safety bottleneck of modern generative models and pretrained policies without requiring policy retraining. In the future, the authors look to extend theoretical guarantees to velocity limits and moving corridor constraints.

sections.heading: Appendix: Formulation extensions (ellipsoids, walls, corridors) and D3IL benchmark results
sections.summary: This section covers extensions of obstacle representations to ellipsoids, polynomial basis degree elevation for half-spaces and corridors, and quantitative evaluations on the D3IL obstacle avoidance benchmark.
sections.details:
### Flexible Extensions of Constraint Blocks
The proposed method accommodates various geometric constraints within the same convex cone framework beyond spherical obstacles:
- **Ellipsoidal Obstacles**: Introducing a weighted norm $\|\mathbf{x}\|_{\bm{\Sigma}}$ enables rotating ellipsoids to be formulated as quadratic blocks.
- **Wall and Corridor Constraints (Half-spaces)**: While boundary walls $\mathbf{a}_w^\top \bm{\gamma}(t) - \xi_w \geq 0$ are degree-$d$ polynomials, applying a Degree Elevation matrix unifies them into the degree-$2d$ cone $\mathcal{K}_{2d}$ used for collision blocks.

### Obstacle Avoidance on the D3IL Benchmark
On an end-effector obstacle avoidance task using a Franka Emika arm (D3IL avoiding-v0, 100 episodes), GlobMP was compared against various diffusion-based planners. When facing obstacles or stay-out zones added abruptly at test time, traditional approaches such as Classifier Guidance and Projected Diffusion struggled with success rates between 20% and 40%. In contrast, GlobMP achieved an outstanding 95% in both task success and safety.

captions.F14: The D3IL benchmark environments (a, b) and a scatter plot of safety rate versus task success rate (c). GlobMP (blue dot) is isolated in the upper-right corner (very high success and safety), outperforming other approaches by a wide margin.
captions.F15: Rollout trajectories across all 100 trials on D3IL, color-coded by constraint-violating trajectories (red) and safe trajectories (dark blue). With GlobMP (bottom center), nearly all rollouts cleanly navigate around test-time stay-out zones (light purple).
captions.F18: Hardware trajectories of 12 robots in a ring swap on the Robotarium Empty environment. While other methods experience congestion and collisions near the center, GlobMP guides the robots to circle and pass each other in an orderly fashion along the perimeter.

takeaways: By replacing discrete time-sampling checks with projections onto the nonnegative polynomial cone, continuous-time safety is strictly guaranteed across every single instant of the motion.

Despite its simple framework of alternating cost gradient descent and convex feasibility projection, GlobMP is theoretically proven to converge to the global optimum as the number of polynomial pieces $N$ increases.
GlobMP functions as a real-time continuous-time "steering" module for pretrained policies (diffusion models or VLAs), dramatically boosting real-world safety without requiring retraining.
limitations: The theoretical global convergence guarantee assumes an initial search over a control point grid; using heuristic initial paths (such as straight lines) in physical deployments could still lead to local minima.
Extending global convergence guarantees to differential constraints, such as velocity and acceleration limits, or complex non-holonomic kinematics remains an area for future work.

When handling large numbers of robots or obstacles, the number of constraint blocks grows quadratically with pairs, requiring GPU parallelization or efficient pruning to run within high-frequency control loops (e.g., 30 Hz).
